newsitem.title: UK: EMI shares rattled by negative broker view.
newsitem.headline: EMI shares rattled by negative broker view.

text.p: In a week when the FTSE 100 index of top British shares has reached record highs, EMI Group Plc -- the world's biggest music publisher and the home of labels such as Apple, Chrysalis and Capitol -- has done the opposite.

EMI shares have plummeted to their lowest since well before last year's demerger of retail arm Thorn, unsettled by negative comment by analysts at investment bank Schroders and worries over the state of the music market.

The stock was down 13 pence at 11.26 pounds ($18.34) at 1610 GMT on Friday, despite the latest FTSE 100 peak, and about seven percent lower than at last Friday's close. But analysts were still reluctant to forecast a rally for EMI.
"I think it might still come down a bit," said one analyst, who asked not to be named. "I'm not convinced we are at the bottom yet."
The analyst noted that EMI shares had a price-earnings ratio of around 26 times, well above the 17 times multiple on the FTSE 100 as a whole.
After tumbling 52-1/2p on Wednesday as word of the Schroders comments spread, EMI shares showed little sign of reviving and on Friday hit 11.22 pounds -- their lowest since October 1995.
Analysts said a 40-page report from Schroders dealt EMI shares the biggest blow of the week.

Schroders initiated coverage of the stock with an "underperform" rating, saying EMI was vulnerable to factors including further strength in sterling, weak European consumer spending and a release schedule which was not outstanding.

Schroders played down the chances of a takeover bid, talk of which helped push the stock up last year, and advised clients that EMI should be sold down to 10.00 British pounds, still about 13 percent below its current level.
Analysts at the brokerage declined further comment.
EMI shares were cast in a different light in August last year, when they leapt to a record 15.10 pounds after the Thorn demerger on August 19.
The decline since then reflects in part a dwindling of takeover hopes and a growing awareness that music sales growth will slow in the current year, analysts said.

Shorn of its relatively unexciting retail operations, including the Radio Rentals British stores chain, EMI was seen as a tempting bid target for global media corporations because of its extensive music publishing business.
Yet shortly after the demerger was approved, EMI chairman Colin Southgate rejected persistant bid talk. Last December EMI said a report of talks with Seagram Co was complete rubbish.

Since then, worries about weak music sales growth have hit the stock, most recently last month when it was shaken by reports that an ailing U.S. music chain had asked suppliers to accept deferred payments.

Analysts said lacklustre music sales growth should by now have been factored into EMI shares -- particularly since EMI said last November it expected current-year sales to grow at slightly below the rate of six to eight percent they foresaw in the medium to long term.
"Everyone has been expecting the third quarter to not be particularly pleasant by comparison with last year, but the reasons have been clear for some time," said another analyst.
Analysts said the market would be looking forward to EMI's next quarterly statement on February 25 for an update on trading conditions. ($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
